Today was the first morning I had to rub and squeeze tight my sleeves to warm my hands. That parched, brisk air.

I like all the seasons. I grew up in Massachusetts, and that is just the way I know.

But,

I've always hated the intensified smell of exhaust the winter brings.

It makes me nauseous and irritable.

I decided to research why this smell is more noticeable during the cold season. According to a couple (1) (2) forums, vehicles’ systems are in place to break down unburnt fuels. These systems and components, like catalytic converters, require higher temperatures to work efficiently. Of course, getting to these levels require more time - i.e., more idling, and releasing higher amounts of fuel. Combustion, as designed, needs a certain amount of oxygen to perform at peak. Engines have an oxygen sensor to detect its levels and to improve performance. The sensors depend heavily on temperature to function. Intro

This is a tutorial on making websites with Flask. It's made to be simple and teach just the working essentials so you can get started and feel confident building upon this foundation.

Installation

Let's assume Python is already installed.

When starting any project, create a virtual environment. Later you will install packages, and it's good practice to have them contained in this environment which is usually initialized in a hidden folder titled .venv/ . In your project folder run this in the terminal:

python -m venv .venv

Now activate your virtual environment by running this command in your terminal:

.\.venv\Scripts\activate

Install Flask with this terminal command:

pip install flask

You're all set for the next page.

static/ - a folder to store your .css file

Many times, people pack for the destination without much consideration of the journey.

Dalam merencanakan perjalanan, aku dulu sering hanya berorientasi pada kenyamanan ketika tiba di tujuan. Membawa banyak barang dengan membayangkan nantinya di tempat tujuan harus merasa senyaman mungkin.

Misalnya ketika hiking, aku membawa perlengkapan lebih banyak demi mendapatkan pengalaman camping yang nyaman. Tidak ada yang salah dengan itu. Hanya saja, semakin sering aku melakukan perjalanan, aku sadar ada biaya yang harus dibayar: kenyamanan ekstra di tempat tujuan sering kali harus dibayar dengan usaha ekstra sepanjang perjalanan.

Aku coba memikirkan kembali tentang ini. Saat hiking, sebagian besar waktu dan tenagaku justru digunakan selama perjalanan, bukan ketika berada di campsite. 🫧 Open on Bubbles

I’ve had the Sculptor 064s for about thee years now and I’ve never given it a proper cleaning. So I decided to do that today.

The process was super easy!

The manual gives the full instructions, but I decided to also make some marks (in dry erase marker) as I went to make sure I didn’t go too far afield with the various moving parts. But the process was super easy:

Remove the adjustment dial face

Unscrew the locator pin and the six hex screws that surround the adjustment plate

Pull out the adjustment plate

Push in on the floppy handle and turn counter-clockwise until the movable burr pops out

After doing that I saw just how low-retention the grinder really is; this is how the burrs looked after 3 years of (admittedly light) use:

So, I just brushed them clean and put them back in.

items.title: I Dosed My Mother-in-Law
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

And she had one hell of a night.

I know it sounds bad, but hear me out. I have a prescription tincture. Per 1 mL, it contains 40 mg of CBD and 10 mg of THC. It’s supposed to help with PTSD. When I take it, I usually stay below 0.5 mL. I’m a lightweight.

My mother-in-law lives on the other side of the city. She comes over once a month or so and stays for a couple of nights. She and my wife get to ramble in Farsi, go shopping, and call all the family in the old country. Loud, and on speaker, of course.

Some time ago, my wife came to me and said, Hey, she wants some stuff to relax. Maybe put some in her evening tea. She’s too embarrassed to say anything to you directly.

Every night, like an old man, I have a lemon-ginger tea. I usually make a cup for her, as well, when she’s here. I started adding around 0.5 mL to her cup.

It’s been months, and I haven’t really noticed much of an effect on her. She still complains about not sleeping well or feeling anxious. So…

items.title: The Urge To Regulate
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
🫧 Open on Bubbles

For roughly a million years our ancestors lived in small bands of 20-50 people, bands which only ever met a few other such bands in their lifetime, other bands with which they had mostly friendly relations. At night, the whole band sat around the campfire, discussing their problems, and agreeing on what to do about them. Problems such as norm violations, and collective decisions like when to move on to a new location.

The highest status went to “thought-leaders” who identified key problems, and suggested solutions on which the group agreed. This process was pretty functional, as these people understood their immediate world pretty well, their elites were in fact better at thinking about such things, and we evolved many ways for groups to think and talk well together.

For the roughly ten thousand years of the farming era, however, we lost much of this. Our groups got larger, were more dominated by leaders who decided for their groups, and interacted lots with…

items.title: Ocarina of Time, again again
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Here’s a thing about nostalgia… Sometimes we put a sheen on an experience that it flourishes beyond the origin — it was better in our mind.

Nintendo took that notion and made it come to life with the latest Ocarina of Time remake.

This is my third go-round with the highly regarded Zelda adventure. The high-def models and environments plus upgraded audio make it feel like remembering something how you wanted it to be all along. It’s pushing emotional buttons while re-wiring memories.

(No real spoilers, but Comparaholic does a great job of illustrating the evolution in this video.)

I’m still early into it, but loving the old-school linear story and cinematic polish.

I haven’t been gaming much this year, so it’s nice to turn off other screens and curl up with this familiar friend as autumn settles into winter.

items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
Note: This is pure personal observation, speculation, and lore-grounded headcanon/fanfiction.

In Chapter 62 of Lotus Eaters, Mamizou explicitly stated that Jo'on used to spread infectious diseases. True to the definition of 疫病神 (Yakubyougami) or Pestilence God, you would normally imagine figures that are sickly and grotesque. In Japanese folklore they usually appear as ragged, sickly old travelers, while in Western imagery and pop culture, the most iconic visuals are plague doctor masks, sickly green skulls oozing goo, or plain medieval sickness.

When I first saw Jo'on in Antinomy of Common Flowers, and read that she is a Pestilence God... well, she certainly looked too sanitized to be one (I mean, ya gotta be a pretty girl to be in Touhou). She was so glamorous, stylish, and clean. As it quickly turns out, her pestilence is more metaphorical than literal: a fever so contagious it causes people to spend impulsively until their bank accounts hit zero.

items.title: Counting seconds
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
When I brew my coffee, I generally do it in 4 parts. One is the blooming phase, I pour 50ml and wait until it's all gone through.

Then I do three other 50ml pours with 10 seconds between each.

To count these 10 seconds, I use crocodiles, like so: "Un crocodile, deux crocodiles, trois crocodiles,...".

Crocodile is the word we use in the french speaking part of Belgium. I think I have seen Americans use Mississippi as well.

I'll use this note as a way to compile all different manners of counting in seconds from around the world. If you could send me an email to tell me how it's done in your part of the world, I'd be very pleased.

Crocodile: Wallonia

Mississippi: USA

items.title: Recommendations for cookbooks that aren't just recipes
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
I'm looking for recommendations for cooking & food books that aren't just sets of recipes, especially ones that are great for just reading through.

The recipes are part of what I want, but I'm also wanting more prose about techniques and history. Some examples which I like along those lines are Samin Nosrat's "Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat" & "Good Things" and Kenji's "The Food Lab" & "The Wok".

Something like Harold McGee's "On Food & Cooking" probably isn't what I want since it's more of a reference book than something to read cover-to-cover.

Any cuisine is good.
